This page covers the exact US occupation O*NET/SOC 21-1091.00, "Health Education Specialists": providing and managing health education programs that help individuals, families, and communities maximize and maintain healthy lifestyles; using data to identify community needs before planning, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating programs designed to encourage healthy lifestyles, policies, and environments; potentially linking health systems, health providers, insurers, and patients to address individual and population health needs; serving as a resource to assist individuals, other health professionals, or communities; and potentially managing health education program funding. Original official scope: Provide and manage health education programs that help individuals, families, and their communities maximize and maintain healthy lifestyles. Use data to identify community needs prior to planning, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating programs designed to encourage healthy lifestyles, policies, and environments. May link health systems, health providers, insurers, and patients to address individual and population health needs. May serve as resource to assist individuals, other health professionals, or the community, and may administer fiscal resources for health education programs. Core tasks listed by O*NET include developing and distributing health education materials, such as reports, bulletins, and visual aids, addressing smoking, immunization, and other public health concerns (importance: 78); developing and maintaining cooperative relationships with agencies and organizations interested in public health care (78); maintaining databases, mailing lists, telephone networks, and other information to support health education program operations (77); documenting activities and recording information such as completed applications, presentations conducted, and persons assisted (76); developing and presenting health education and promotion programs, such as training workshops, conferences, and school or community presentations (75); collaborating with health specialists and civic groups to determine community health needs and service availability and develop goals to meet needs (71); developing, conducting, or coordinating health needs assessments and other public health surveys (71); supervising professional and technical staff implementing health programs, objectives, and goals (71); developing operational plans and policies necessary to achieve health education objectives and services (70); providing program information to the public through press releases, media campaigns, or program-related websites (70); developing and maintaining health education libraries to provide resources for staff and community agencies (68); designing and conducting evaluation and diagnostic studies to assess health education program quality and performance (66); writing, preparing, and coordinating grant applications and grant-related activities to obtain funding for health education programs and related work (66); providing guidance to agencies and organizations on health education needs assessment and program development and implementation (62); designing and implementing training programs for new staff and organizing continuing education for current staff (60); and developing educational materials and programs for community agencies and local and state governments (71). Common titles include Certified Diabetes Educator, Health Educator, Health Education Specialist, Health Promotion Specialist, Public Health Educator, Community Health Consultant, Health Education Coordinator, and Education Coordinator. Wage, employment, and industry figures on this page use this occupation's own scope as presented on O*NET's 21-1091.00 page, which does not label them as drawn from a parent or broader occupation and shows projected growth for 2024–2034 as "Faster than average (5% to 6%)" (faster than average), with a Bright Outlook designation. See the sections below for scope and boundaries.

Practice scenario | An entirely fictional community health education program task package (for practicing the process only; it represents no real organization, community, population, data, or funding). Draft a plan addressing: (1) how to organize a health education program using a fictional community health needs survey and population and behavioral risk description, with a structured approach covering target populations and needs identification; data, methods and sources; evidence and behavioral theory; goals, indicators and measurable definitions; activities, channels and materials; implementation and partner collaboration; evaluation, monitoring and improvement; and ethics, informed consent and privacy. Specify information gaps requiring supplementation, including population composition, health literacy, language and culture; baseline data and indicator scope; evidence-based interventions and behavioral theory; channel reach and accessibility; evaluation methods and samples; and grants, budgets and funding sources. (2) How to design completion and review points for a fictional program implementation and evaluation record form, covering fields and definitions; target populations, coverage and reach; activities, dose and fidelity; indicators, baselines and results; anomalies, adverse events and referrals; and original records and revision trails. (3) How to write a program description suitable for handover: needs and goals—evidence and theory—activities and channels—evaluation and indicators—budget and resources—ethics, privacy and outstanding items. (4) How to record and retain program, evaluation, beneficiary, and grant records, distinguishing disclosable information from controlled materials or those involving personal health information and protected health information. (5) How to pause, review, and escalate when data are insufficient or evidence and conclusions do not align, the program deviates from its evidence base, adverse events or ethical and privacy risks arise, medical, diagnostic, or medication advice is involved, or the role's authorization is exceeded. Use public materials and simulated data; do not use real population data or personal health information.

Fit signals | US O*NET 21-1091.00 work activity importance scores identify communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates (95), establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships (93), updating and using relevant knowledge (92), getting information (88), interpreting the meaning of information for others (88), communicating with people outside the organization (87), performing for or working directly with the public (86), scheduling work and activities (86), training and teaching others (86), making decisions and solving problems (84), and organizing, planning, and prioritizing work (84) as this occupation's most important activities. Work context data (response percentages) show email every day for 100%, face-to-face discussions every day for 88%, telephone conversations every day for 77%, constant contact with others for 76%, working with or contributing to a work group or team extremely important for 61%, very great freedom to determine tasks, priorities, and goals for 49%, dealing with external customers or the public extremely important for 40%, working indoors in environmentally controlled conditions every day for 69%, high responsibility for others' health and safety for 50%, being exact or accurate very important for 34%, public speaking at least weekly for 50%, and regular schedules for 71%. If you are willing to design and promote health programs using data and evidence, communicate with communities, organizations, and stakeholders, and accept responsibility for health education quality and population health literacy, this occupation's daily requirements may align more closely with your working style.

This occupation focuses on designing, implementing, and evaluating health education and promotion programs and managing funding. An error in needs identification or the evidence base, materials or messages inconsistent with science, inaccurate data or evaluation scope, statements crossing into medical, diagnostic, or medication advice, or mishandling protected health information or personal health information can cause misinformation, damaged trust, and compliance and legal risks. O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed, SVP 7.0 to less than 8.0). The education section on that page shows an associate's or other two-year degree for 62%, a bachelor's degree for 31%, and a high school diploma or equivalent for 3%. US projected growth for this occupation on this page in 2024–2034 is "Faster than average (5% to 6%)" (faster than average), with a Bright Outlook designation. If you find it difficult to sustain public-facing communication and promotion, bear responsibility for others' health and safety and consequences of error, or accept responsibility for the integrity of evidence, data, and privacy compliance, treat these as practical costs requiring careful consideration.

Taking responsibility for judgment | Real fit depends on whether you can accomplish three things together in the same health education program: do the professional work thoroughly (design, implement, and evaluate programs using population needs, data, evidence, and behavioral theory, cite knowledge consistent with current evidence, and produce usable program, evaluation, and beneficiary records); manage compliance, ethics, and boundaries (work and keep records under public health and health education ethics, informed consent, privacy, and data requirements; distinguish disclosable information from controlled materials or those involving protected health information or personal health information and handle them under established rules; and avoid crossing into medical, diagnostic, or medication advice); and accept clearly defined job responsibilities (be accountable for your needs identification, program design, implementation, evaluation, and records, and refer matters beyond authorization or involving clinical judgment, medical advice, policy, and major funding decisions to the appropriate roles or organizations under established rules). Test this through a verifiable experience, such as completing a health education program plan and evaluation, indicator, and recordkeeping notes for a fictional task, or reviewing the handling of a program deviation or ethical and privacy risk, rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire's conclusion.

Direct answer | The health education specialists covered here are the exact occupation O*NET 21-1091.00 (Health Education Specialists). Their work falls into several categories: (I) Needs identification and assessment—use data to identify community needs before planning; develop, conduct, or coordinate health needs assessments and other public health surveys; and collaborate with health specialists and civic groups to determine community health needs and service availability. (II) Program design and materials—develop and present health education and promotion programs, such as training workshops, conferences, and school or community presentations; develop and distribute health education materials, such as reports, bulletins, and visual aids; develop educational materials and programs for community agencies and local and state governments; and develop and maintain health education libraries. (III) Implementation and partner collaboration—develop and maintain cooperative relationships with agencies and organizations concerned with public health care; supervise professional and technical staff implementing health programs, objectives, and goals; and design and implement training for new staff and organize continuing education for current staff. (IV) Evaluation and improvement—design and conduct evaluation and diagnostic studies to assess health education program quality and performance; document activities and record information, such as completed applications, presentations conducted, and persons assisted. (V) Funding and policy—write, prepare, and coordinate grant applications and grant-related activities to obtain funding; develop operational plans and policies needed to achieve health education objectives and services; and potentially manage program funding. (VI) Communication and advocacy—provide program information to the public through press releases, media campaigns, or program-related websites; and guide agencies and organizations on health education needs assessment and program development and implementation. The work cycle connects needs identification and assessment—program design and evidence base—implementation and partner collaboration—evaluation and improvement—funding and policy—communication, advocacy, and review. This page does not conflate the occupation with adjacent community health workers, dietitians and nutritionists, health informatics specialists, postsecondary health specialties teachers, healthcare social workers, rehabilitation counselors, social and community service managers, or social and human service assistants. Nor does it expand health education program responsibilities to replace clinical diagnosis, treatment, medication, or medical decisions.

Mainland China scope and gaps | Mainland China has roles similar to health education specialists in health education, health promotion, public health, community health, chronic disease management, and occupational health, such as health education professionals, health promotion and health management practitioners, community health and public health service personnel, and chronic disease management specialists. Their work, qualifications, standards, and records are governed by the Law of the People's Republic of China on Basic Medical and Health Care and the Promotion of Health, Law of the People's Republic of China on Prevention and Treatment of Infectious Diseases, Law of the People's Republic of China on Prevention and Control of Occupational Diseases, Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China, national basic public health service specifications, and relevant health education and health promotion specifications. Basic public health and health education services must follow specifications and standards; diagnosis, treatment, and medication must be handled by appropriately qualified organizations and personnel; residents' health information and personal health information must be legally protected and processed on a minimum-necessary basis. However, this round did not obtain a nationwide occupational wage distribution exactly corresponding to US O*NET 21-1091.00 (Health Education Specialists). The National Bureau of Statistics publishes average wages of persons employed in urban units by industry category, an industry-level scope without occupational distinctions or a separate listing for this occupation. Under the evidence policy, this page records only statistical scopes and visible gaps (marked "Insufficient evidence:"), without using industry averages, advertised recruitment pay, or US wages to extrapolate starting salaries, medians, or individual income across jurisdictions. The Chinese and US scopes differ in legal environments and statistical periods; they are neither combined nor converted.

Ethics and privacy notes | Organize work under public health and health education ethics, privacy, and data protection requirements. Program materials and messages must align with current evidence and identify evidence sources and limitations; they must not replace clinical diagnosis, treatment, medication, or medical advice. Population and individual data must follow informed consent, minimum necessity, purpose limitation, and de-identification principles. Protected health information or personal health information must be accessed, stored, and shared under organizational and legal requirements. Work involving vulnerable and special populations must follow ethical review, accessibility, and language access requirements. Activities and materials must undergo required review before release. Immediately pause and escalate for review under established rules when data are insufficient or evidence and conclusions do not align, programs deviate from their evidence base, adverse events or ethical and privacy risks arise, or medical advice or matters beyond authorization are involved. Standards and quality boundaries | This page involves three types of requirements. Professional practice and quality: needs assessments, program design, materials, and evaluations must use population data, evidence, and behavioral theory, with program, evaluation, and beneficiary records maintained. Ethics and privacy: programs must follow informed consent, minimum necessity, and purpose limitation; protected health information or personal health information must be managed under organizational and legal requirements; and medical, diagnostic, or medication advice must not be provided beyond the role's scope. Records and information: program, evaluation, beneficiary, and grant records must be truthful, complete, and traceable. Controlled materials or those involving personal health information, as well as externally disclosed information, must be managed through approval and minimum necessity. This page offers general reminders only and does not constitute medical, diagnostic, treatment, medication, legal, or public health policy advice.

Immediately pause when data are insufficient or evidence and conclusions do not align, programs deviate from their evidence base, adverse events or ethical and privacy risks arise, or records differ from site conditions. Escalate within your authorization and request review by ethics, compliance, medical, or clinical roles. Do not modify records or add entries retrospectively on your own authority.

Boundary conclusion | This page covers O*NET 21-1091.00 (Health Education Specialists). The core differences from adjacent roles lie in subjects, outputs, and levels of authority. This occupation focuses on population health needs and health education program design, implementation, evaluation, and funding, producing needs assessments, program plans, materials, evaluation, beneficiary, and funding records based on evidence and data definitions. The basis is public health, health education, and health promotion specifications and organizational program, ethics, and data rules.

This occupation's authority and approval | Routine needs assessments, program design, implementation, evaluation, and communication must remain within ethics, standards, and organizational authorization. Clinical judgment, medical advice, major policy and funding decisions, and processing and disclosure of protected health information must follow qualification and approval requirements. Obtain approval from the relevant roles or organizations or hand over matters under established rules; do not make judgments or grant release approval beyond your authority.

Limits of conclusions in adjacent roles | Conclusions in the same group and adjacent roles are mostly limited to the project and responsibilities concerned and usually do not constitute determinations of health outcomes, medical diagnoses, or legal liability. Cross-disciplinary conclusions and those involving clinical matters, major disclosures, or policy and funding decisions have limits on their applicability.

This occupation's conclusion boundaries | Program and evaluation conclusions state only verifiable needs, data, indicators, activities, fidelity, and result records, distinguishing measured facts, judgments and inferences, and matters awaiting verification. Do not make unauthorized judgments or commitments on matters beyond your authority (clinical judgment, medical advice, major policy and funding decisions, and processing and disclosure of protected health information). If data are insufficient or evidence and conclusions do not align, programs deviate from their evidence base, adverse events or ethical and privacy risks arise, or records differ from site conditions, pause and escalate or hand over. Conclusions must also withstand review by supervisors, ethics and compliance roles, funders, and regulatory inspections.

paragraphs: Conclusion | The core differences between this occupation (O*NET 21-1091.00, Health Education Specialists) and adjacent roles lie in subjects, outputs, and levels of authority. This occupation focuses on population health needs and health education program design, implementation, evaluation, and funding, producing needs assessments, program plans, materials, evaluation, beneficiary, and funding records based on evidence and data definitions. Community Health Workers (21-1094.00) focus on community health service linkage, support, and follow-up; Dietitians and Nutritionists (29-1031.00) on nutrition assessment and dietary prescriptions; Rehabilitation Counselors (21-1015.00) on rehabilitation assessment, counseling, and employment support; Health Informatics Specialists (15-1211.01) on health data and information systems; and Social and Human Service Assistants (21-1093.00) on direct service assistance. Their subjects, outputs, and levels of authority differ. Authority for clinical judgment, medical advice, and major policy and funding decisions cannot be carried across roles.

Evidence note | The occupations compared below come from O*NET occupational classifications and public materials to help distinguish adjacent occupations' work and assess selection fit. They do not establish qualification, hiring, or pay conclusions, nor constitute medical, diagnostic, treatment, medication, legal, or public health policy advice. Each occupation's wages and employment must be checked separately under its own SOC scope. This table makes no numerical comparison and does not use one occupation's wages as a proxy for another. Qualification, ethics, and data requirements must be checked under each jurisdiction's and organization's requirements. Introduction | The following comparison uses four columns: career track—core work and outputs—key differences—which choice is a better fit. Health education programs, community services, nutrition, case work, and health data often connect within the same public health or healthcare organization, but connection does not imply interchangeability. When moving between tracks, learn the new track's subjects, standards, data, authorization, and responsibility boundaries.

Key differences: this occupation focuses on population health needs and health education program design, implementation, evaluation, and funding. It designs and evaluates programs and provides materials and recommendations within ethical and authorization boundaries using evidence, data, and behavioral theory, taking responsibility for program quality, ethics, and records. Other roles center on community health service linkage, nutrition assessment and diets, rehabilitation counseling and employment support, health data and information systems, or direct service assistance. They usually have more specialized standards, qualifications, and subjects and do not bear primary responsibility for population health education program design, evaluation, and funding (but must collaborate with this occupation and clarify boundaries).

Better suited to people willing to design and promote health programs using data and evidence, communicate with communities, organizations, and the public, and accept responsibility for population health literacy and program ethics and quality.

Core work and outputs: use data to identify community needs before planning; conduct health needs assessments and public health surveys; design and present health education and promotion programs and materials; develop and maintain partnerships with agencies and civic groups; supervise program teams; design and conduct evaluation and diagnostic studies to assess program quality and performance; write and coordinate grant applications; communicate program information to the public; and train staff. Outputs are needs assessments, program plans, materials, evaluation, beneficiary, and funding records based on evidence and data definitions (O*NET/SOC 21-1091.00).
This occupation: Health Education Specialists (O*NET/SOC 21-1091.00)

Key differences: community health workers focus on community health service linkage, support, follow-up, and advocacy, producing community service and follow-up records. This occupation focuses on needs assessment, program design, implementation, evaluation, and funding for population health education, producing needs assessments, program plans, and evaluation records. Individual case follow-up and service linkage are usually not its main duties (but it must collaborate with community health workers to reach populations).
Better suited to people who want to conduct community visits, health service linkage, and follow-up; this occupation emphasizes needs assessment, program design, implementation, and evaluation.

Core work and outputs: conduct community health outreach, screening, referrals, and follow-up, link health and social services, and keep service and follow-up records. Outputs are community service and follow-up records.
Community Health Workers (21-1094.00)

Key differences: dietitians and nutritionists focus on nutrition assessment, dietary prescriptions, and nutrition therapy, producing nutrition assessments and dietary plans. This occupation focuses on population health education needs assessment, program design, implementation, and evaluation, producing program and evaluation records. It usually does not bear primary responsibility for clinical nutrition assessment and dietary prescriptions (but must collaborate with dietitians and nutritionists to ensure accurate nutrition information).

Better suited to people who want to conduct clinical or public nutrition assessments and dietary interventions; this occupation emphasizes population health education program design, evaluation, and promotion.

Core work and outputs: perform and record nutrition assessments, dietary interventions, and nutrition therapy using nutrition science and dietary guidelines. Outputs are nutrition assessments and dietary plans.
Dietitians and Nutritionists (29-1031.00)

Key differences: rehabilitation counselors focus on rehabilitation assessment, counseling, and employment support, producing rehabilitation assessment and counseling records. This occupation focuses on population health education programs and evaluation, producing program and evaluation records. It usually does not bear individual case responsibility for rehabilitation assessment and employment support (but must collaborate with rehabilitation counselors to connect services).

Better suited to people who want to provide rehabilitation assessment, counseling, and employment support; this occupation emphasizes population health education needs assessment, programs, and promotion.
Core work and outputs: conduct and record rehabilitation needs assessments, counseling, rehabilitation planning, and employment support. Outputs are rehabilitation assessment and counseling records.
Rehabilitation Counselors (21-1015.00)

Key differences: health informatics specialists focus on health data, information systems, data standards, and reports, producing health data, systems, and reports. This occupation focuses on population health education programs and evaluation, producing program and evaluation records. It usually does not bear primary design and operational responsibility for health information systems and data standards (but must collaborate with health informatics specialists to use data accurately).

Better suited to people who want to work with health data, information systems, and data standards; this occupation emphasizes population health education program design, implementation, and evaluation.

Core work and outputs: collect and govern health data according to data standards, design and use health information systems and reports, and safeguard privacy. Outputs are health data, systems, and reports.
Health Informatics Specialists (15-1211.01)

Key differences: social and human service assistants focus on direct service assistance, visits, and records, producing assistance and records. This occupation focuses on population health education programs and evaluation, producing program and evaluation records. It usually does not bear primary responsibility for direct daily living assistance and companionship (but must collaborate with social and human service assistants to support program implementation).
Better suited to people who want to provide direct service assistance, visits, and companionship; this occupation emphasizes needs assessment, program design, implementation, and evaluation.
Core work and outputs: provide and record visits, assistance, companionship, and referrals for individuals and families according to service plans. Outputs are assistance and records.
Social and Human Service Assistants (21-1093.00)

paragraphs: The six cards identify conditions requiring review, pausing, or handover. They are editorial synthesis, without accident rates for this occupation. Check clinical, funding, and disclosure authority by specific matter and organizational requirements.

Direct answer | The core occupational risk is not merely whether activities can be completed, but four types of failure with serious consequences. Health and information failure: needs identification, the evidence base, or materials and messages inconsistent with science can cause misinformation; statements crossing into medical, diagnostic, or medication advice may mislead populations, harm health, and damage trust. Ethics and privacy failure: inadequate informed consent, minimum necessity, or handling of protected health information or personal health information, insufficient de-identification, or sharing beyond permitted boundaries may cause privacy breaches and compliance and legal risks. Quality and evaluation failure: inappropriate program design, implementation fidelity, evaluation methods or definitions, or inaccurate records may cause ineffective programs, wasted resources, and misjudged performance. Authorization and collaboration failure: independently making clinical judgments, giving medical advice, making policy and funding decisions, or disclosing externally beyond authorization; single-point dependence for critical certifications or data capabilities; and unclear standards with communities, organizations, and funders on scope, responsibility, and disclosure boundaries can cause disputes. Work context data—constant contact with others for 76%, public speaking at least weekly for 50%, high responsibility for others' health and safety for 50%, and consequences of error that are extremely serious for 19%, serious for 23%, and fairly serious for 27%—provide context for the seriousness of these consequences.

O*NET supports the occupational task context. The six cards are editorial scenarios, not indicators of frequency, card-by-card legal determinations, or occupational risk scores. Check personal information processing requirements separately by jurisdiction, legal basis, and specific matter.

Needs, evidence, and materials must be evidence-based and reflect current evidence, with sources and limitations identified. Refer clinical judgments and medical advice to appropriately qualified roles. Immediately stop, review, and report inconsistent evidence or statements beyond scope.

Scenario | Program materials contain content inconsistent with current evidence or potentially involving medication advice. Deadlines are tight, and stakeholders want publication first and corrections later.

Within China, first verify a lawful processing basis, clear purposes, and necessary scope. Medical and health information is subject to sensitive information rules; check consent, notification, and protection requirements for the specific matter. De-identification does not automatically exempt responsibility; check other jurisdictions separately.

Scenario | Special populations or sensitive health information are involved, but authorization and informed consent are incomplete. Under schedule pressure, staff are asked to collect and share first and complete formalities later.
You and program and evaluation roles; program quality and compliance consistency

Inappropriate program design, implementation fidelity, evaluation methods or definitions, inaccurate records, or improper handling of adverse events and referrals; may cause ineffective programs, wasted resources, misjudged performance, and harm to rights and interests

Define and document program and evaluation methods in advance. Truthfully record dose, fidelity, coverage, and results, and refer and report adverse events under established rules. Program and evaluation records must be truthful, complete, and traceable.

Scenario | Evaluation data have missing values or inconsistent definitions. As a milestone approaches, program stakeholders demand effectiveness conclusions using existing data first, with additional measurements and revisions later.
You, ethics and compliance roles, and funders; conclusion and disclosure boundaries

Independently making clinical judgments, giving medical advice, making major policy and funding decisions, or disclosing externally beyond authorization, or conclusions beyond evidence and methodological support; may trigger legal, compliance, ethical, and trust disputes

Policy and funding decisions and external disclosures require procedural approval and records. Conclusions must align with evidence and ethics; refer matters beyond authorization to the appropriate roles or organizations. When asked to exceed authorization or provide definitive conclusions, first explain the boundaries and hand over through the prescribed process.

Scenario | Staffing is tight, and the organization asks personnel without authorization for the matter to independently give clinical advice, make major funding decisions, or disclose information externally.
You and team and certification roles; program continuity and compliance consistency

Single-point dependence for critical certifications, data or evaluation capabilities, or partnerships; leave, program peaks, or certification expiry interrupt programs and evaluations or create inconsistent definitions. May cause program delays and compliance and quality risks.

Establish backup, handover, and update rules for certifications, data capabilities, partnerships, and materials. Critical program and evaluation experience must be reproducible and documented. Report shortages of staff, capability, or certification under established rules and adjust priorities.

Scenario | The only key staff member familiar with a program type, evaluation, data, and partnerships is on leave, and untrained personnel are asked to take over critical programs and evaluations temporarily.

Insufficient adaptation to population composition, health literacy, language, and culture, inadequate accessibility or protection of vulnerable populations, or inequitable program impacts; may cause insufficient reach, health inequalities, and harm to rights and interests

Editorial advice is to check language, culture, health literacy, and access channels and implement protection and necessary review under the legal or organizational requirements applicable to the specific program. Do not treat every health education activity as research requiring ethical review.

Scenario | The target population's language, health literacy, and accessibility needs have changed, but the program still uses old materials that people cannot understand or access, and reported problems are not reviewed.

subject.summary: Health education specialists correspond to the exact occupation O*NET/SOC 21-1091.00, "Health Education Specialists": providing and managing health education programs that help individuals, families, and their communities maximize and maintain healthy lifestyles; using data to identify community needs before planning, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating programs; potentially connecting health systems, health providers, insurers, and patients to address individual and population health needs; serving as a resource to assist individuals, other health professionals, or communities; and potentially managing program funding. Core tasks include conducting health needs assessments and surveys, developing and presenting health education and promotion programs and materials, developing and maintaining partnerships, designing and conducting evaluation studies, writing and coordinating grant applications, and communicating program information to the public. Common titles include Health Educator, Health Education Specialist, Health Promotion Specialist, and Certified Diabetes Educator. Original official scope: Provide and manage health education programs that help individuals, families, and their communities maximize and maintain healthy lifestyles. Use data to identify community needs prior to planning, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating programs designed to encourage healthy lifestyles, policies, and environments. May link health systems, health providers, insurers, and patients to address individual and population health needs. May serve as resource to assist individuals, other health professionals, or the community, and may administer fiscal resources for health education programs. Scope note: US wage and employment data on this page use this occupation's own scope (21-1091.00) as presented by O*NET on its 21-1091.00 page (not labeled there as drawn from a parent occupation), without substituting adjacent occupations' figures. Projected growth for this occupation in 2024–2034 is 5% to 6%, with a Bright Outlook designation, and O*NET places it in Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed, SVP 7.0 to less than 8.0). This page does not constitute medical, diagnostic, treatment, medication, legal, or public health policy advice.
